title: The catacombs and the fish
hook: the Greek word for fish spells Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nero's fire: a rumor, a crowd, and Christians made to carry the blame. Your line was blamed for the fire. Did you hear a whole group blamed for something? Day seven hundred.

Two curved lines, crossing at one end to make a tail. It's on the back of cars in traffic, on necklaces, on the sign of a plumber who wants you to know something about him. Now go underground, into the tunnels outside the walls of ancient Rome, where Christians buried their dead. On the plaster, by lamplight, the same creature shows up again: a fish, sometimes swimming beside a basket of bread. Today's word is that fish, and it's hiding a sentence.
screen: `TWO CURVED LINES.` → `TUNNELS OUTSIDE ROME.` → `A FISH BESIDE THE BREAD.`

segments.voice: The Greek word for fish is ichthys. Spell it in Greek capitals and each letter starts a word: Iesous, Jesus. Christos, Christ. Theou, of God. Huios, Son. Soter, Savior. Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior. A whole creed, folded into one small animal. Saint Augustine noticed it and explained it in The City of God, so by his time the word game was known. Second, why a fish fit so well. The Gospels are full of them. Jesus calls fishermen from their boats, in the Douay-Rheims: "Come ye after me, and I will make you to be fishers of men." He feeds a crowd with loaves and a few fish. Third, the water. The writer Tertullian called Christians little fishes, born in water after the example of their Fish, Jesus Christ. He meant baptism: born in water, and like fish, kept alive by staying in it. Fourth, the catacombs themselves. Films sometimes show Christians living down there in hiding. They were cemeteries: long tunnels of graves, where families came to bury and to pray, and where painters put their hope on the walls. The fish beside the bread is read by some as a picture of the Eucharist. And the secret sign? A story people tell says one Christian would draw half a fish in the dirt, and a stranger who finished it was a friend. It's hard to trace that story to any early writer. But the fish did work like a secret sign in a deeper way. To someone outside, it was only a fish. To someone who knew the letters, it was a confession of faith, hidden in plain sight.
screen: `FIVE LETTERS, FIVE WORDS.` · `FISHERS OF MEN.` · `LITTLE FISHES, BORN IN WATER.` · `CEMETERIES, NOT HIDEOUTS.` · then, large: `JESUS CHRIST, SON OF GOD, SAVIOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: draw a small fish. Paper is good. A fingertip on your palm or on the table works too. Two curved lines, crossing at the tail. Then settle, and breathe. Go through the five words slowly, one for each breath: Jesus. Christ. Son. Of God. Savior. If you're Catholic, notice which word you live by easily and which one you rarely think about. If you're learning, simply notice how much one little drawing was made to hold. If you pray, you can let the words be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Ichthys. Greek for fish, and a sign whose letters spell Jesus Christ, Son of God, Savior. Today's word.
Your line: the secret sign. Today, look out for a fish on a car, a door or a necklace, and remember the sentence inside it. Day seven hundred.

howItsDone: Some Catholics wear or display the fish as a sign of faith, and the early Christian paintings of fish and bread in the Roman catacombs can still be visited today.

notes: Matthew 4:19 Douay-Rheims (Challoner) wording: confirm exact text.
Augustine, City of God 18.23, discusses the acrostic in connection with the Sibylline verses; confirm the reference and the claim that the word game was known 'by his time'.
Tertullian, De Baptismo 1 ('we, little fishes, after the example of our ICHTHUS Jesus Christ, are born in water') paraphrased: confirm.
Reading the fish-and-bread paintings as Eucharistic is attributed to 'some'; some art historians read some of them as funerary meals. Keeper to confirm wording.
The half-fish-in-the-sand story is presented as a story people tell without early documentation; confirm.
Pronunciation ikh-THOOS follows a common reconstructed Greek reading; Keeper may prefer ICK-thoos as commonly said in English.
